item.title: PM to visit slain child's Pallabi home Thursday night
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is scheduled to visit the residence of seven-year-old child, who was recently killed in a brutal rape and murder incident in Pallabi, Dhaka, on Thursday night.
Party sources said the prime minister was expected to meet the grieving parents at their home in Pallabi, Mirpur around 9:30pm, following a meeting of the party’s standing committee.
According to police, the victim child's body was recovered on Tuesday morning from beneath a bed inside a neighbour’s flat. Her severed head was later found in a bathroom. A murder case was subsequently filed at Pallabi Police Station.
Law enforcement officials first detained the wife of the prime accused, identified as Swapna Akter. Later, the main suspect, Sohel Rana, was arrested in connection with the case. He was subsequently produced before a court, where he reportedly gave a confessional statement admitting to the rape and killing of the child.
The incident has sparked widespread public outrage across Bangladesh, with human chains, protest rallies and demonstrations held in Dhaka and several districts, demanding swift justice and the maximum punishment for those involved.

item.title: Seven-year-old girl murder: classmates, locals protest demanding justice
item.description:
The entire nation has been left in deep shock and mourning following the brutal killing of a seven-year-old girl in Dhaka’s Pallabi area. Grief has engulfed her family, teachers, and classmates while her parents remain inconsolable over the devastating loss of their only daughter.
On Thursday morning, the girl’s father Abdul Hannan Molla visited his daughter’s classroom at Popular Model School in Mirpur where she studied in Class Two. The girl had consistently performed at the top of her class, securing second place in playgroup and KG and ranking first in class one.
Entering the classroom filled with children of his daughter’s age, he broke down in tears and embraced her classmates. His tears created a deeply heartbreaking atmosphere across the entire classroom. Her classmates, struggling to hold back tears, said she would never be forgotten and demanded exemplary punishment for those responsible.
Teachers and students of the school later formed a protest rally in Pallabi, carrying banners “We demand justice” calling for swift and strict punishment for the perpetrators.
Protesters blocked roads in Mirpur on Thursday afternoon, demanding the maximum punishment for those involved in the rape and murder of seven-year-old girl.
The demonstrators staged the blockade at Mirpur 10 and 12, bringing traffic on the stretch to a standstill.
During the protest, they chanted slogans such as “Justice, justice, we want justice,” “We demand justice,” “Why was our sister killed,” “Destroy the den of criminals,” and “We demand death penalty for the accused,” among others.
Inside the family home, the girl’s academic trophies now stand as silent reminders of her short but promising life. Her elder sister repeatedly looked at the awards and spoke of her sister’s dedication and brilliance in studies.
Public anger over the incident has also spilled onto the streets. Residents gathered outside the family home and later staged demonstrations at Pallabi Police Station, expressing outrage and demanding the harshest punishment. Many voiced grave concerns over child safety, saying that insecurity has now become a daily fear for families.
The protest movement has spread beyond the capital, with human chain demonstrations and rallies reported in several districts. In the child’s ancestral village in Sherpur, local volunteers under the banner of “Aajker Tarunno” also held protests demanding the maximum punishment for those responsible.
Police recovered the slain child’s body from a flat in Pallabi on Tuesday and later found additional remains from a bathroom in the same residence.
A murder case was subsequently filed at Pallabi Police Station. Authorities initially detained the wife of the main suspect, Swapna Akter, before arresting the primary accused, Sohail Rana.
Following his arrest, Sohel Rana reportedly gave a confessional statement in court, admitting to the killing after the alleged assault.
The incident has reignited nationwide outrage and intensified calls for stronger child protection measures and the swift delivery of justice.

item.title: Salahuddin : Govt wants Sheikh Hasina back through legal procedure
item.description:
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed has said the government wants to bring back former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina to Bangladesh through legal procedures and existing extradition mechanisms.
“We want Sheikh Hasina back through legal procedure. Through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and under the existing extradition treaty, a formal request has been made for her return so that she can face the cases filed in Bangladesh,” he said.
Speaking at a press briefing on the country’s law and order situation at the home ministry’s conference room in Bangladesh Secretariat Thursday, the minister said a formal request had already been sent through diplomatic channels for her return so that she can face legal proceedings in Bangladesh.
Responding to another question on India’s Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA) and the National Register of Citizens (NRC), the minister said those are entirely India’s internal matters.
“India’s CAA or Assam’s NRC are their own legal and administrative matters concerning their citizens. There is no scope for Bangladesh to comment on those issues,” he said.
However, the minister added that Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) remains on high alert along the border to prevent any kind of illegal infiltration or push-in.
He also said the government remains committed to maintaining law and order and ensuring justice through lawful and institutional processes.

item.title: Measles outbreak: Death toll 488 as seven children die in 24 hours
item.description:
Bangladesh’s measles outbreak continued to worsen as seven more children died in 24 hours till 8am Thursday, raising the total death toll to 488 since March 15, according to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS).
Of the latest deaths, four were classified as suspected measles-related fatalities while three were laboratory-confirmed, the bulletin said.
Chittagong recorded the highest number of deaths among reporting areas.
Since March 15, the country has recorded 405 suspected measles deaths and 83 confirmed deaths.
During the same period, 1,423 new suspected measles cases were reported, taking the total number of suspected infections to 59,279.
During the same period, 208 new confirmed measles cases were detected, raising the cumulative number of confirmed infections to 8,275.
According to the bulletin, 46,407 suspected measles patients have been admitted to hospitals since March 15, while 42,336 patients have been discharged after recovery.

item.title: Finance Minister: Govt pursuing welfare state through economic reforms
item.description:
Finance Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury on Thursday said the government has undertaken an all-out reform program to establish a welfare state by moving away from an ‘oligarchic and patronage-driven’ economic system.
The minister said democratization of the economy is not merely a slogan but the core philosophy of the present government, he said while addressing a roundtable discussion titled “Budget in Times of Crisis and Public Expectations” at a hotel in Dhaka.
He said special emphasis is being placed on bringing marginalized groups including rural blacksmiths, potters and weavers into the mainstream economy after they remained outside the budgetary framework for decades.
The finance minister said the upcoming national budget would include special projects and fund allocations to promote and monetize the creative economy, including theatre, culture, music, painting and artificial jewellery.
He also announced plans to establish “theatre districts” in major cities beyond Dhaka and said Bangladesh’s culture, films and music would be branded and promoted globally to strengthen the country’s soft power, following examples set by neighbouring countries.
Amir Khosru said the government is taking strict measures to reduce the cost of doing business, including excessive charges and bureaucratic harassment at ports and across the supply chain.
He said the number of approvals required for business operations and project implementation would be reduced to 13, down from what he described as an excessively complicated system.
The minister added that the entire economic and administrative system would be brought under digital automation within the next year, while initiatives are underway to introduce a “One Citizen, One Card” system for all public services.
Highlighting plans for financial sector reforms, the finance minister said the government is strengthening the capital and bond markets as alternatives to high-interest bank loans.
He said international investment bankers, fund managers and the International Finance Corporation (IFC) have shown strong interest in the initiative.
On taxation, Amir Khosru said the government would verify the actual market share of multinational and major tobacco companies, including The Coca-Cola Company and PepsiCo, to ensure fair tax collection and prevent tax evasion.
He said plans are also underway to introduce a simplified flat-rate tax system for small restaurants and shop owners to bring them under the tax net and reduce harassment by tax officials.
The finance minister said sweeping changes are being introduced in tax policymaking through a proposed bill that would establish a policy-making body comprising individuals with expertise in the global economy, local trade and human profitability, rather than focusing solely on tax collection.
Urging people to remain patient for the next two years, he said the government’s goal is not only to increase GDP growth but also to ensure that the benefits of growth improve the lives of ordinary citizens.

item.title: Swapon seeks UK, Swiss cooperation in ensuring media freedom
item.description:
Information and Broadcasting Minister Zahir Uddin Swapon has said the present government is committed to ensuring the freedom of media.
“The government is determined to ensure media freedom. To this end, work has already begun to form a Media Commission,” he said. He made the remarks when British High Commissioner in Bangladesh Sarah Cooke paid a courtesy call on him at his office in the Secretariat on Thursday.
State Minister for Information and Broadcasting Yasser Khan Choudhury, MP was present at that time.
The minister sought cooperation from the United Kingdom in this regard.
During the meeting, Sarah Cooke congratulated Zahir Uddin Swapon on assuming charge as information and broadcasting minister. The minister expressed interest in utilizing the experience of the UK media regulatory authority Office of Communications (Ofcom), saying “Ofcom’s experience can be utilized in formulating media sector policies in Bangladesh.”
The British High Commissioner assured the minister of giving all necessary cooperation in this regard and informed him about the overall activities of Ofcom.
Later, Swiss Ambassador in Bangladesh Reto Renggli paid a courtesy call on the information minister at his office.
During the meeting, the Swiss Ambassador also congratulated Zahir Uddin Swapon on assuming his new responsibility.
The information minister said, the government is committed to ensuring media freedom. At the same time, we want to protect people from misinformation and disinformation.
To address the challenge, he stressed the importance of Switzerland’s modern experience and technological assistance.
At the meeting, State Minister for Information and Broadcasting Yasser Khan Choudhury said, “While Artificial Intelligence (AI) has opened up new possibilities in the world today, it has also created a major global challenge in the fields of information verification and security.”
He called on all concerned to work together in addressing the challenge.
At the same time, the state minister invited the Swiss ambassador to invest in Bangladesh’s potential sectors.

item.title: Ain o Salish Kendra flags surge in child abuse, rape, killings
item.description:
The Ain o Salish Kendra (ASK) has expressed deep concern over a recent surge in cases of child abuse, rape, and murder in Bangladesh, stating that the killing of seven-year-old Ramisa Akter in Pallabi along with other recent incidents has once again exposed the severe weaknesses in the country’s child protection system.
In a statement sent to the media, the human rights organization said these incidents are not isolated crimes but rather a reflection of systemic failure in state protection mechanisms and a broader crisis of social accountability.
Citing its own statistics, Ain o Salish Kendra (ASK) reported that between January and May 20, 2026, at least 118 children were subjected to rape, while at least 46 children were victims of attempted rape. In addition, at least 17 children were killed either after rape or following failed rape attempts during the same period.
The organization noted that Articles 28 and 32 of the Bangladesh Constitution guarantee children’s rights to life, safety, and dignity. It also highlighted that the National Children Policy 2011 enshrines the state’s commitment to ensuring the best interests, protection, and non-discriminatory development of children. Bangladesh, as a signatory to the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, is also legally bound to prevent all forms of violence, sexual abuse, and exploitation against children. Despite these legal and policy frameworks, ASK said prolonged judicial processes and weak investigations continue to obstruct justice for child victims. As a result, grieving families not only endure deep trauma and insecurity but also increasingly lose confidence in the justice system.
ASK stressed that every case of child abuse and murder must be treated with the highest priority, ensuring swift judicial resolution. It also called for fully independent, transparent, and impartial investigations to prevent any political or social influence from undermining justice.
The organization further urged strengthened state monitoring and protection mechanisms to ensure children’s safety in educational institutions, homes, and digital spaces. It also emphasized strict enforcement and regular oversight of existing child protection laws.
Concluding its statement, ASK said child protection is not merely a policy commitment but a constitutional responsibility of the state, a fundamental human rights obligation, and a basic benchmark of a civilized society. Failure to ensure children’s safety, it warned, is not only a legal failure but also a moral and humanitarian one that undermines the state’s credibility.

item.title: Lightning kills 6 in three districts
item.description:
Six people were killed in lightning strikes in Naogaon, Barisal and Natore districts on Thursday.
According to reports, three people were killed in Naogaon, two in Barisal and one in Natore.
In Naogaon, three people, including two farmers, were killed in separate lightning strike incidents in Raninagar upazila on Thursday.
Two farmers were killed when lightning struck them while they were harvesting paddy amid rain at Jathail in the upazila.
The deceased were identified as Akkas Fakir, 60, son of late Asad Fakir, and his relative Tarek Fakir, 24, son of Aminul Islam Fakir of Paroil village in Raninagar upazila.
Zakaria Mondal, Officer-in-Charge of Raninagar Police Station, said the two farmers died on the spot after being struck by lightning while working in a paddy field during rain.
Police later recovered the bodies and handed them over to the families, he said.
Meanwhile, Nayan Talukdar of Guata Atnitapra village was killed after being struck by lightning while bringing cattle back from a field amid rain around 11am, the OC added.
Raninagar Upazila Project Implementation Officer (PIO) Nazrul Islam said Tk 20,000 would be provided to each of the victims’ families through the local administration.
In Barisal, two workers at a betel leaf garden were killed and another injured after lightning struck them while they were working at a garden in Mahilarar Bhimer Par area of Gournadi upazila around 2pm, said Tarique Hasan Russel, Officer-in-Charge of Gournadi Model Police Station.
The deceased were identified as Abu Taleb Hawladar, son of Alim Hawladar, and Sukanto Bala, 38, son of Mukunda Bala of Uzirpur upazila in the district.
The injured person was taken to Gournadi Upazila Health Complex.
In Natore, a 60-year-old brick kiln worker was killed and another injured after lightning struck them while they were working at a brick field in the Sirajipur area of Lalpur upazila.
The deceased was identified as Esken Ali of the upazila.
Shafiqul Islam, Officer-in-Charge of Lalpur Police Station, said the two workers fell unconscious after being struck by lightning during a storm in the morning.
Later, they were taken to Lalpur Upazila Health Complex, where doctors declared Esken Ali dead.

item.title: Fakhrul: Strong social movement needed alongside law to prevent rape
item.description:
LGRD and Cooperatives Minister Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir underscored the need for waging a strong social movement alongside application of law to prevent social menace rape.
In a Facebook post from his verified page, he strongly condemned the recent several rape incidents describing it as a sign of moral degradation.
“The incidents of rape, child abuse, and murder are not isolated events; rather, they are a horrifying reflection of years of moral decay, social irresponsibility, and the rapid decline of human values,” he said adding “We are committed to making every possible effort against this inhumane crime”.
Fakhrul, also BNP secretary general, said the government is committed to continuing comprehensive efforts against this inhumane crime.
He said only laws or government initiatives alone are not enough. “What is needed is a strong national social movement. Families, schools, madrasas, teachers, religious leaders, the media, social organizations, and every citizen must come forward,” he said.
He underlined teaching children about respect, humanity, responsibility, and the dignity of women. “Ensuring the safety of our children means securing the future of Bangladesh. Let us all join together in this struggle for change,” he said.

item.title: Home minister: Police will soon file charge sheet in Ramisa murder case
item.description:
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said that police will submit a chargesheet soon in the murder case of child Ramisa, after an accused was arrested within 24 hours of the incident.
Speaking at the Secretariat on Thursday, he said the main accused in the case is possibly Sohel Khan, who has been arrested along with his wife.
He said: “They gave a statement under Section 164. We can assure you that our side will complete a proper investigation and submit the chargesheet within a short time.”
Salahuddin Ahmed said people often discuss justice in the context of delays in trials, but that is not always the case.
He said some trials are delayed, which creates the impression that justice may not be delivered.
He added that such crimes had also taken place during the interim government’s tenure, and legal and judicial action was taken within a short time in those cases.
He said he could only assure that an exemplary trial would be completed as quickly as possible, but he could not say what the punishment would be.
He said: “We are not in the Middle Ages now. We are in the modern era, and law reform is an ongoing process. Laws must be updated and made timely according to society’s needs. Those are continuing processes. We will certainly need to make some amendments in different laws. We will look into that.”
He also said it is important to consider whether very quick trials can sometimes lead to injustice, or whether the strictest laws may later be misused.
Salahuddin Ahmed said it is not right to create a law or establish a court in haste every time an incident occurs.
He said: “We have to look at this on a broader canvas. For example, an incident took place in Magura. There was an uproar over it, and perhaps some legal amendments were brought in and the trial was completed within a short time. That was a demand of the time. But what will happen in the long term, and what will not, must also be considered.”
He further said that in cases of child rape, a court was established and a tribunal was formed, but it later became possible to give the same jurisdiction to women’s and children’s courts without increasing the number of courts.
He said this was because of issues related to revenue expenditure, court setup and manpower. He said it would otherwise be seen that courts were set up in 64 districts even though some districts might have two cases, some 10, and some none.
He said arrangements should be made in a way that ensures both public safety and justice. But he added that it was not right to quickly enact laws or create courts in all matters just to ease public anger for a short time.
He said the home ministry has responsibilities in reducing crime and carries out proactive work in that regard.
He said: “For example, anti-drug drives are continuing, and drives against extortion and terrorism are also under way. These are largely proactive measures so that crimes decrease. But in crimes like rape and murder, I can talk about the police’s activities after the incident has occurred. Since we took charge, in every heinous crime of this kind, can any of you say that the police did not make the maximum effort and could not arrest the accused within a short time? There is not a single one. I have all the lists. If there is any deviation, you can raise the question.”

item.title: A friend in New Zealand
item.description:
We are encouraged by recent discussions between leaders from Bangladesh and New Zealand that have highlighted broader economic cooperation.
Of particular interest is Wellington expressing interest in continuing duty-free and preferential market access facilities for Bangladesh even after the country eventually graduates from the least developed country (LDC) category -- an opportunity that Bangladesh cannot afford to overlook.
New Zealand is undoubtedly a high‑value market with strong standards, and its willingness to deepen ties should be taken as expressing confidence in our potential.
With that said, this is a relationship that can and must go beyond trade preferences, one that encompasses investment, technology transfer, and collaboration in renewable energy and agriculture - all areas where New Zealand has expertise and Bangladesh has urgent needs.
Bangladesh must also now ensure that its own policies align with the opportunity to deepen ties, not just with New Zealand but all other nations it is seeking to diplomatically engage with. That means, above all else, building the capacity to meet the quality benchmarks required for these ties to deepen. We cannot be a nation that inks deals and furthers conversation, only for them to fall short as a result of our inability to take them to the next level.
Bangladesh must also ensure that such cooperation benefits ordinary citizens.Trade and investment must translate into jobs, skills, and sustainable growth at home and not remain abstract, benefiting only a narrow circle.
Bangladesh’s economic diplomacy must look beyond traditional partners. As such, a stronger relationship with New Zealand can and must evolve from duty‑free access into a strategic partnership that strengthens resilience and broadens opportunity.

item.title: A free press contributes to good governance
item.description:
The meeting earlier this week between leaders of the Editors’ Council and Prime Minister Tarique Rahman once again was a reminder of the fragile state of press freedom in Bangladesh.
The reality is that the media continues to operate under pressure - legal, political, and economic - that undermines its ability to serve the public.
Our record on press freedom has long been troubling, with journalists facing harassment, intimidation, and censorship. Laws have continued to be used to silence criticism, while ownership structures and political influence compromise editorial independence.
This has all resulted in a media landscape where self‑censorship is widespread and fearless journalism is rare.
With that said, we are encouraged that the prime minister directed the Information Ministry to complete examinations on issues raised so the government could take a “visible step” and we are equally encouraged by the Editors’ Council announcing plans to formulate and adopt a journalists’ code of conduct for self-regulation and the intention to develop more accountability mechanisms.
Press freedom is not a privilege to be granted but rather a right enshrined in democracy and is a hallmark of good governance. A state that values accountability must allow the press to question, investigate, and criticize without fear.
The government must therefore move beyond assurances, and ensure, above all else, that repressive laws are reformed, independent oversight strengthened, and protections for journalists guaranteed. Economic pressures on media houses must also be addressed, so that financial vulnerability does not translate into editorial compromise.
Our nation cannot aspire to democratic maturity while the press remains constrained.

item.title: Female worker missing after boat capsizes in Jamuna
item.description:
A female worker went missing on Thursday after a boat capsized in the Jamuna River during a sudden storm in Dhunat upazila of Bogra.
The incident took place around 11:30am near the Baniajan Spur area. The boatman and nine other female workers were rescued alive, officials said.
According to police, fire service officials and local residents, 10 women labourers crossed the river by boat from Baniajan Spur Ghat in the morning to work in cornfields on the Sanbandhar char. However, rain disrupted their work, forcing them to return.
As the boat neared the spur area on its way back, strong winds and heavy rainfall triggered a whirlpool in the river, causing the vessel to capsize.
Hearing the news, local villagers rushed to the scene and joined rescue efforts with members of the Dhunat Fire Service and Civil Defence. Rescuers managed to save the boatman and nine workers, but Anguri Khatun, 50, wife of Lal Mia from Goshaibari cluster village, remained missing.
Md Zahurul Islam, acting station officer of Dhunat Fire Service and Civil Defence, said search operations were continuing in the Jamuna River to locate the missing woman.
He added that a diver team from Rajshahi Fire Service would be called in if she is not found soon.

item.title: 441 new sailors join Navy with pledge to serve the nation
item.description:
A total of 441 recruits of the A-2026 batch formally joined the Bangladesh Navy after successfully completing their boot camp training at the Sher-e-Bangla Parade Ground in Patuakhali on Thursday. The colorful passing-out parade marked the conclusion of their rigorous training and their formal induction into the naval force, said an ISPR press release.
Chief of Naval Staff Admiral M Nazmul Hassan attended the ceremony as chief guest, where he inspected the parade and took the salute. He later distributed awards among the best-performing recruits.
Md Shahriar Tutul earned the prestigious “Navy Chief Medal” as the Best All-Round Sailor for achieving excellence in both professional and academic performance. Md Samiul Islam Shakil secured second place and received the “Comkhul Medal,” while Md Kader Mia won the “Sher-e-Bangla Medal” for third place. Among female recruits, Mosammat Maria Akter received the “Pritilata Waddedar Medal” as the Best Female Sailor.
Addressing the parade, the Navy Chief paid tribute to the martyrs of the Liberation War, including Bir Sreshtho Ruhul Amin and Lt Commander Moazzem Hossain. He highlighted the Navy’s ongoing modernization efforts, including the addition of helicopters, unmanned aerial vehicles, hydrographic survey vessels, and anti-drone systems.
He also praised naval personnel for supporting civil administration, maintaining law and order, and performing duties during the 13th national parliamentary election in remote coastal regions.
Senior officers of the Principal Staff Officers (PSOs) of Naval Headquarters, high-ranking military and civil officials, distinguished persons from the Patuakhali, Barisal, and Khulna regions, and the guardians of the newly inducted sailors were present at the parade ceremony.

item.title: Garment workers stage demos in Gazipur demanding Eid holiday and May salary
item.description:
Garment workers staged protests in Sreepur upazila of Gazipur on Thursday, demanding 11 days of Eid-ul-Azha holiday, payment of overdue overtime wages, full salary for May, and the removal of several factory officials. The demonstration later turned violent, leading to clashes with police.
The incident took place around 9:30 am at KSS Knit Composite Ltd in Baherarchala area. According to workers, they had been staging protests for several days over their demands and submitted them to factory authorities on Wednesday. However, when workers arrived at the factory on yesterday morning, they found a closure notice posted at the gate along with a heavy police presence, triggering tensions.
Workers alleged that police prevented them from entering the factory and used batons when they attempted to force their way inside. This led to a chase and counter-chase between workers and police. Police later fired sound grenades and teargas shells to disperse the demonstrators. Several workers were reportedly injured during the clash.
The factory management, however, claimed that some workers from the sewing section had engaged in an illegal strike without prior notice on May 19 and 20, obstructed other employees from working, threatened senior officials, and disrupted production. Citing deteriorating law and order conditions, the management announced the factory’s indefinite closure under Section 13(1) of the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006.
In an official notice signed by General Manager (HR and Administration) AM Nurul Amin, the company stated that it had already announced 10 days of Eid leave and 20 days’ advance salary for workers.
Gazipur Industrial Police Superintendent Amzad Hossain said police brought the situation under control after dispersing the protesters with sound grenades and tear gas. He added that the situation is now calm and additional police have been deployed at the factory.

item.title: Interim chief: Sri Lanka cricket finances 'greater than feared'
item.description:
Financial irregularities surrounding Sri Lankan cricket were far worse than feared, government-appointed administrators said Thursday, promising a full accounting and sweeping reforms.
"We have already ordered a forensic audit of the accounts," Eran Wickramaratne, interim president of Sri Lanka Cricket (SLC), told his first news conference since taking office last month.
He said financial irregularities were "far greater than initially feared".
He said the new SLC leadership -- handpicked by the government of President Anura Kumara Dissanayake -- would bring in sweeping reforms as concerns linger over international sanctions.
The current administration was appointed following the mass resignation of SLC's elected officials last month -- a move that raised fears of possible suspension by the International Cricket Council (ICC) over political interference.
The SLC, the country's richest sports body, was suspended for two months in 2023 on similar grounds.
Wickramaratne, however, said discussions with the ICC were underway on reforming the SLC.
"Our talks with the ICC have been extremely cordial and constructive," he said.
"We have been very open and transparent in what we are doing, and they want us to pursue open and transparent methods in doing this."
Reforms include drafting a new constitution aimed at curbing abuses that allowed groups to retain power for a prolonged period, he added.
Four-time SLC president Shammi Silva and his entire committee stepped down in April after the government intervention, clearing the way for the current overhaul.
The previous administration had also faced criticism over the national team's performances, including an early exit from the T20 World Cup, which Sri Lanka co-hosted with India earlier this year.

item.title: Kings retain Federation Cup Title as Dorielton hits hat-trick
item.description:
Brazilian forward Doriellton Gomes produced a brilliant hat-trick as Bashundhara Kings retained the Federation Cup title with a thrilling 3-2 victory over Mohammedan Sporting Club in the final held at the Bashundhara Kings Arena on Wednesday. Mohammedan took the lead twice in the first half and went into the break with a 2-1 advantage, but Doriellton's second-half brilliance helped Kings complete a dramatic comeback and secure the trophy.
The Brazilian striker scored twice after the interval and finished the entire Federation Cup campaign with an impressive tally of 12 goals.
Mohammedan made an early breakthrough when Uzbek midfielder Muzaffar Muzaffarov opened the scoring in the 5th minute. However, the lead lasted only a few minutes as Doriellton equalized from the penalty spot in the 9th minute.
Forward Sourav Dewan restored Mohammedan's lead in the 34th minute, giving the traditional black-and-white outfit a narrow advantage at halftime.
After the restart, Bashundhara Kings fought back strongly. Doriellton leveled the score once again in the 50th minute before completing his hat-trick with the winning goal in the 80th minute.
Mohammedan attempted to respond in the closing stages but failed to find another equalizer.
With the victory, Bashundhara Kings once again demonstrated their dominance in domestic football by securing a domestic treble for the second time since joining the country's top-flight league.
Earlier this season, Kings won the Challenge Cup title and also reclaimed the Bangladesh Premier League championship, continuing their remarkable run of success in Bangladesh football.

item.title: DR Congo cancel World Cup training in Kinshasa amid Ebola outbreak
item.description:
The Democratic Republic of Congo national football team have cancelled a planned pre-World Cup training camp at home after the country was hit by an Ebola outbreak, a team official told AFP Wednesday.
The outbreak of the highly contagious haemorrhagic fever was declared in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo last Friday.
The 17th Ebola outbreak to hit the DRC is already suspected of having caused 139 deaths from around 600 probable cases.
The training camp that "was due to begin in Kinshasa for three days" has been "relocated" to Belgium, a team press officer told AFP, without confirming whether the Ebola outbreak was the reason for the decision.
"No players based domestically have been selected" for the national squad, he added.
DR Congo have qualified for the World Cup, which will be held in the United States, Mexico and Canada, for only the second time after playing in 1974, when the country was known as Zaire.
They have planned to be based in Houston during the tournament, where they will play their first Group K match on June 17 against Portugal.
DR Congo are then scheduled to head to Guadalajara to play Colombia on June 24 before returning to the United States to play Uzbekistan in Atlanta on June 28.
A US official said Tuesday the team would be able to travel to play in the World Cup.
The United States has banned non-Americans who have been in the DRC, Uganda or South Sudan in the previous 21 days from visiting due to the outbreak.
The US official said the DR Congo had already been training in Europe so may not have been subject to the ban in any case.
But if they in fact were in DR Congo over the last 21 days, they would be subject to strict screening of the sort required for returning American citizens -- not a complete ban.

item.title: South Korea coach 'hurt' by support for North team
item.description:
Suwon FC Women's coach has said his team felt "hurt" by a lack of home support after losing to the first North Korean sports team to visit the South in eight years.
South Korea's Suwon went down 2-1 to North rivals Naegohyang Women's FC in Wednesday's Asian Women's Champions League semi-final, which was played at Suwon's home stadium.
Interest in the rare North-South match was intense, and 7,087 general admission tickets sold out within hours of going on sale last week.
The official attendance for the game, which was played in torrential rain at the roofless Suwon Sports Complex Stadium, was 5,763.
A large group of spectators from civic groups backed by Seoul's unification ministry were in the stadium to support both teams.
Naegohyang's arrival at South Korea's Incheon International Airport on Sunday saw players and officials surrounded by throngs of reporters and supporters holding welcome signs.
Suwon coach Park Kil-young said the huge attention surrounding the game had affected his players.
"We are Suwon FC Women of the Republic of Korea," he said, struggling to control his emotions.
"Throughout the match, our players and our staff felt hurt."
There were no official away supporters at the game because North Koreans are generally not allowed into the South and the two countries have technically remained at war since 1950.
Suwon were backed by fans banging drums and chanting for their team.
Park said his team had "never played in front of so many people and so many writers before".
"We needed to win today to draw more attention to women's football here, and our players competed so hard with that in mind," he said.
"Hopefully, this match will help people take more interest in our sport and make them come to more matches."
Naegohyang came from behind to win the game and book their place in Saturday's final against Japan's Tokyo Verdy Beleza, which will also be played in Suwon.
Suwon spurned a chance to equalise with just over 10 minutes to play when captain Ji So-yun missed a penalty.
Naegohyang coach Ri Yu Il said the atmosphere in the stadium had contributed to the occasion.
"It was a very intense match and we were too caught up in it to be too conscious of the cheering," said Naegohyang coach Ri Yu Il, who formerly led North Korea's women's national team.
"However, I felt that people here have such a high level of interest in football."

item.title: Nadal says he sought honesty, transparency in Netflix documentary
item.description:
Tennis great Rafael Nadal says he sought to be "transparent" and "honest" in his forthcoming Netflix documentary series, speaking to AFP at a preview event ahead of its release.
The series from the streaming giant will be available from May 29, during the French Open - the Grand Slam tournament where the Spaniard forged his legend with a record 14 titles.
"I believe it's a genuine documentary that doesn't paint everything in rosy colours, and combines my sporting career with the difficulties I have faced," Nadal told AFP shortly before the screening of the first of four episodes in Madrid.
"I think I've been quite transparent about my life and everything that has happened to me. I've been honest, and it's my story," added the undisputed king of clay, who won 22 Grand Slam titles over a career spanning more than 20 years before retiring at the end of 2024.
Rafael NadalRafael Nadal in action on clay at the French Open in Paris. Photo: photosport The documentary was filmed during that final season, "while I was still playing, trying to come back from injury and hip surgery", he said.
"And I didn't succeed. I tried to stay competitive, but I couldn't get back to 100 percent. That whole process was filmed: the doubts, the uncertainty, and then acceptance of the situation."
Asked whether it was important for him to tell that difficult final chapter, Nadal replied: "Not necessarily, but I have people around me that I trust who convinced me to do it - people who have been successful in this industry and perhaps had a broader view of my career."
"I followed their advice and here we are. I hope people will like it," added Nadal, who bid a tearful farewell last year to Roland Garros, where a mark of his footprint is carved into the clay on Court Philippe Chatrier.

item.title: Midland Bank, BB sign deals to support local CMSMEs
item.description:
Midland Bank PLC. (MDB) has signed a participation agreement with Bangladesh Bank to implement the Tk3,000 crore cluster financing scheme and the Tk1,500 crore financial sector fund for the development of micro, small, and medium enterprises (FSFDMSME).
The initiative aims to promote entrepreneurship and support the sustainable growth of cluster-based and CMSME enterprises across Bangladesh.
The agreement signing ceremony was held on May 18, 2026, at the Jahangir Alam Conference Hall of Bangladesh Bank.
Nurun Nahar, deputy governor of Bangladesh Bank, attended the event as chief guest.
Nawshad Mustafa, director of SMESPD of Bangladesh Bank, and Imtiaz U Ahmed, managing director & CEO of Midland Bank PLC, signed and exchanged the agreement documents on behalf of their respective organizations.
Under the agreement, Midland Bank PLC. will provide financing facilities to eligible cluster entrepreneurs and CMSME enterprises at a concessional interest rate of 7% under Bangladesh Bank's refinance scheme.
Both term loans and working capital financing facilities will be available to support the growth and expansion of small businesses and entrepreneurs across the country.
The initiative is expected to enhance financial inclusion, encourage entrepreneurship development, generate employment opportunities, and strengthen the CMSME sector, which plays a vital role in Bangladesh’s economic growth and development.
Among others, Mohd Javed Tarek Khan, head of institutional banking division; Ahsan Jamil Hossain, head of SME Division of Midland Bank PLC; and senior officials from Bangladesh Bank and Midland Bank PLC were also present at the ceremony.

item.title: Experts: Reforms should not be limited to slogans
item.description:
Economists have stressed the need for effective implementation of reforms, not just words, to restore the country's economic growth and ensure long-term stability.
According to them, it is not possible to address the current challenges of the economy without structural changes in the banking, revenue, trade and investment systems.
These views emerged at a seminar organized by the Policy Research Institute of Bangladesh (PRI) in Banani, the capital, on Thursday. At the event, economists, businessmen and policymakers discussed the upcoming budget, productivity growth and priorities for economic reforms.
Fahmida Khatun, executive director of the Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD), said: "Reforms should not be limited to slogans. Various initiatives were taken during the past non-political governments, but there was no major success in practical implementation."
She said that the government's big challenge is to ensure that important sectors like banking, energy and infrastructure do not fall under the influence of any particular group or 'mafia system'.
At the same time, she mentioned the slow pace of development project implementation and the unbridled increase in operating expenses as worrying for financial discipline.
Khatun said that the ADP implementation rate during July-March of the current fiscal year was only 36.19%, which is the lowest in the last five years.
She commented that both time and cost are increasing due to the delay in project implementation. She also suggested ensuring a competitive environment in the market instead of relying solely on contractionary monetary policy to control inflation.
PRI chairman Zaidi Sattar said that the current tariff structure of Bangladesh is at a very unreasonable level. In his words, "The average tariff is about 55%. It is not possible to conclude an effective free trade agreement with any country by maintaining this high tariff rate."
He further said that Bangladesh has been talking about free trade agreements for the past two decades but has not been able to sign any significant agreement so far. Although the open trade system is one of the reasons for the low prices of goods in the international market, Bangladesh is still deprived of that benefit.
The main paper of the seminar was presented by PRI Principal Economist Ashikur Rahman. He said that it is not possible to achieve sustainable growth by increasing government expenditure or increasing market demand alone. For this, a productivity-based new growth model is needed.
According to him, the basis of the new growth model should be the development of the investment environment, resolving the energy crisis and effective reform of state institutions.
Highlighting the need for reform of the revenue system, former NBR chairman Nasiruddin Ahmed said that if the responsibility of formulating tax policy and collecting tax is in the hands of the same institution, there is a conflict of interest. Therefore, he emphasized the need to separate tax policy and tax administration.
He cited the example of India and called for an end to harassment of taxpayers along with the introduction of a simplified tax system for small service providers and bike riders.
Highlighting the crisis in the private sector, former president of Dhaka Chamber of Commerce and Industry Shams Mahmud said that a few influential groups have controlled the banking sector in the last decade. While they laundered money with low-interest loans, ordinary entrepreneurs are now struggling to run their businesses under the pressure of high interest rates.
He demanded strengthening the long-term and easy-to-use financing system to meet the challenges of post-LDC transition.

Second-grade student Ramisa was allegedly raped and killed on Tuesday by a tenant living in a neighbouring flat in Pallabi.

Police said suspect Sohel Rana allegedly called the child into his room after she left her home in the morning. There, Sohel allegedly raped and subsequently killed her.

Later, Ramisa's dismembered body was recovered from beneath a bed, while her head was found inside a bucket kept in the bathroom of Sohel's flat.

item.title: Ensuring access to digital services for persons with disabilities is our priority: ICT Minister
item.description:
Minister for Posts, Telecommunications and Information Technology Faqir Mahbub Anam said that ensuring equal access to digital services for persons with disabilities is one of the government’s key priorities.

As part of the celebration of Global Accessibility Awareness Day (GAAD) 2026, Aspire to Innovate (a2i) organised an event today, Thursday, at the BIDA Auditorium in Agargaon, Dhaka. Friendship and Sightsavers co-organised the event, said a press release.

State Minister for Social Welfare Farzana Sharmin; Sightsavers Country Director Amrita Regina Rosario; and Ayesha Taasin Khan, Senior Director and Head of Inclusive Citizenship Sector at Friendship, attended the event as special guests. Valerie Ann Taylor, Founder of Centre for the Rehabilitation of the Paralysed (CRP), attended as guest of honour. The event was chaired by Quazi Anowar Hossain, Secretary of the ICT Division, while Md Abdur Rofiq, Project Director (Additional Secretary) of a2i, delivered the welcome remarks. Abdullah Al Fahim, Head of Programme Management, moderated the event, and accessibility consultant and visionary disability rights advocate Vashkar Bhattacharjee also spoke.

Faqir Mahbub Anam said, “Accessible websites and apps have been developed keeping in mind the principle that no one should be left behind. From now on, all digital services will be designed considering the needs of persons with disabilities. Because this is not a matter of charity; we see it as their right. Technology must be aligned with people’s needs, abilities and diversity.”

He further said, “Through new technologies, we want to connect persons with disabilities more actively with the mainstream of society. We want to turn the children of our country with disabilities into assets. The ICT Division will take all necessary initiatives to ensure a dignified position for persons with disabilities in society through technology.”

Farzana Sharmin said the government will provide full support for the growth of public and private institutions and innovative initiatives that contribute to digital accessibility. Ensuring universal accessibility is essential to building a Bangladesh for all. The government is working so that all citizens, including persons with disabilities, can easily access digital services.

The ICT secretary said Bangladesh’s digital progress will only be complete when every citizen can use digital services with dignity, independence and equality. To achieve this, government institutions, development partners, civil society, organizations of persons with disabilities, technology innovators and the private sector must work together in a coordinated manner.

In his welcome remarks, Md Abdur Rofiq said that although a significant number of people in the country live with some form of disability, they still do not receive the full benefits of digital services in many areas. To ensure the digital inclusion of persons with disabilities, a2i is working to gradually make government digital services accessible. He also mentioned plans to develop AI-based sign language tools, make e-commerce and e-learning platforms more inclusive, and establish a Disability Innovation Knowledge Platform for knowledge sharing.

Vashkar Bhattacharjee said, “Bangladesh first—if everyone has digital access. This is not charity; it is our constitutional right.” He added that a2i’s Disability Innovation Lab is working as a specialized initiative to ensure digital accessibility. The lab is advancing inclusive innovation in areas such as government digital services, educational materials, skills development, employment, entrepreneurship development and awareness raising. Alongside the initiative to ensure Accessibility Level A on government websites, initiatives such as multimedia talking books, accessible dictionaries and MuktoPaath have created new opportunities for students and citizens with disabilities.

Amrita Regina Rosario said Sightsavers has long been working in Bangladesh to eliminate avoidable blindness, establish the rights of persons with disabilities, and support the implementation of inclusive policies. Their “Equal Bangladesh” campaign is bringing together organizations of persons with disabilities and civil society to advocate for rights-based inclusion.

Ayesha Taasin Khan said true inclusion is ensured only when technology, services and opportunities are equally accessible and usable for everyone. Friendship is working to ensure equality, accessibility and meaningful participation for all, including persons with disabilities, and to deliver innovative essential services to persons with disabilities living in climate-vulnerable and hard-to-reach remote areas.

At the event, five initiatives were recognized. These were the Ministry of Social Welfare’s Therapy Service Management for Persons with Disabilities and Disability Information System; Bangladesh Police’s Online Police Clearance Certificate Service; the Gram Adalat Mobile App of the Local Government Division and UNDP; and Eastern Bank’s EBL Skybanking initiative.

In addition, Minister Faqir Mahbub Anam visited various innovators’ stalls set up around disability-friendly innovations in the morning, while Rehan Asif Asad, Adviser to the Honorable Prime Minister on Posts, Telecommunications and Information Technology, visited them in the afternoon. After visiting the stalls, they expressed appreciation for the innovations and highlighted the government’s goodwill and commitment to building an inclusive Bangladesh for all. Other guests and senior officials from the relevant organizations were also present.

Global Accessibility Awareness Day is observed worldwide every year on the third Thursday of May. Its aim is to make websites, mobile apps, software and digital services easier to use and accessible for persons with disabilities. As a signatory to the United Nations Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities and the Marrakesh Treaty, Bangladesh is committed to ensuring digital inclusion. At the same time, digital accessibility is receiving importance under the Rights and Protection of Persons with Disabilities Act and the government’s policy priorities.

item.title: Country’s only disease hospital now a health risk itself
item.description:
Bangladesh’s only specialized infectious disease hospital is battling severe overcrowding, unhygienic conditions and critical resource shortages even as it treats some of the country’s deadliest contagious diseases, raising fresh concerns over patient safety and infection control during the ongoing measles crisis.
The Infectious Diseases Hospital in Mohakhali -- the country’s main referral facility for infectious diseases -- is now treating measles, AIDS, tetanus, chickenpox, rabies, kala-azar, malaria and anthrax patients in the same overcrowded wards and corridors because of severe space shortages.
During a visit on Thursday, measles patients were found occupying wards, corridors and spaces near lifts on multiple floors of the hospital, while children and their caregivers crowded nearly every available area.
Hospital data showed that although the facility has only 15 designated measles beds, 51 measles patients were admitted that day alone.
At the same time, the 100-bed hospital was also treating AIDS, rabies, tetanus, chickenpox and other infectious disease patients.
Public health experts warn such conditions significantly increase the risk of cross-infection inside a hospital specifically meant to contain contagious diseases.
One patient, 11-year-old Asma Akter from Kishoreganj, was first admitted with chickenpox.
After recovering and returning home, she later contracted measles and had to be readmitted to the same hospital.
Relatives of patients described scenes of overcrowding and poor sanitation, saying many attendants are forced to sleep inside corridors because of bed shortages.
One guardian said they had to buy a small fan themselves because corridor areas lacked ventilation.
Visits to different floors revealed scattered waste, overflowing spaces and inadequate cleaning arrangements.
Relatives alleged that sanitation work is often carried out only once daily despite the hospital’s heavy infectious disease load.
This year alone, 1,875 patients with measles symptoms have sought treatment at the hospital.
Among them, 1,124 required admission and 406 were confirmed measles cases. At least 43 patients have died with measles or measles-like symptoms during the same period.
Hospital Superintendent AFA Asma Khanom acknowledged the severe limitations facing the facility.
She said only 19 sanitation workers currently serve the entire hospital, making it impossible to maintain proper hygiene standards.
“I am trying from my position,” she said.
“Even though efforts are being made to improve the environment, the desired change cannot be achieved.”
She also admitted that because of space shortages, patients suffering from different infectious diseases are often treated together.
The hospital’s location inside the densely populated Sat Tola slum area of Mohakhali has further complicated management and infection control, officials said.
Public health expert MA Bari warned that infectious disease hospitals should ideally remain isolated from densely populated communities to reduce transmission risks.
“Infectious diseases can spread from person to person. The denser the population around such a hospital, the higher the risk becomes,” he said.
Experts also warned that overcrowded and unhygienic conditions inside infectious disease facilities can themselves become sources of infection if immediate interventions are not taken.
With Bangladesh already struggling through its worst measles outbreak in decades, health experts say the deteriorating conditions at the country’s only specialized infectious disease hospital expose broader weaknesses in the country’s public health infrastructure.

item.title: Eid cattle markets heat up as prices soar in Dhaka
item.description:
With Eid-ul-Azha only days away, cattle markets across Dhaka are rapidly filling up as truckloads of sacrificial animals enter the capital, but traders and buyers alike are bracing for another season of soaring prices driven by rising feed costs and mounting transport expenses.
Although most temporary cattle markets are still in preparation mode and buyer crowds remain relatively thin, traders say the real rush will begin within the next two to three days as office holidays start and Eid shopping peaks.
Visits to major markets including Gabtoli, Diyabari, Shahjahanpur and Amulia showed rows of newly arrived domestic cattle from northern, southwestern and char regions, while workers rushed to build bamboo enclosures, unload animals and secure prime selling spots.
This year’s prices, however, are already alarming many buyers.
Traders at Gabtoli -- the capital’s largest cattle market -- said small cows that sold for around Tk1 lakh last year are now being priced at nearly Tk1.5 lakh, while medium-sized cattle are rarely available below Tk2.5 lakh.
Farmers and traders blamed the sharp increase mainly on soaring cattle feed prices and higher rearing costs over the past year.
Still, many traders admitted current prices are being intentionally kept high early in the season as sellers try to gauge market demand before large numbers of buyers arrive.
“In the beginning, everyone asks higher prices,” one trader said.
“The market will become clearer once buyers start coming in bigger numbers.”
Authorities expect the pressure on Dhaka’s cattle markets to intensify sharply from next week as thousands more sacrificial animals arrive from across the country.
According to official estimates, more than 3,600 livestock markets will operate nationwide this year, including over two dozen in the capital alone.
Dhaka North and South city corporations have already completed leasing most temporary market sites and say trading will continue for five days before Eid.
According to the Department of Livestock Services, Bangladesh has around 12.33 million sacrificial animals available this year against an estimated demand of 11.63 million, leaving a projected surplus of more than 2.2 million animals nationwide.
Despite that surplus, many city residents fear prices may remain beyond the reach of middle-income buyers if demand surges during the final days before Eid.
Meanwhile, authorities say special measures have been taken to prevent illegal roadside markets, improve waste management and maintain order inside the temporary cattle trading zones.
Abdus Salam, administrator of Dhaka South City Corporation, said no unauthorized cattle markets would be allowed this year.
“No market lease has been given outside the rules,” he said, adding that preparations have been completed to ensure smooth trading and proper waste disposal during Eid operations.

item.title: ‘We do not want people dependent on allowances’
item.description:
State Minister for Women and Children Affairs and Social Welfare Farzana Sharmin Putul says the government is moving to reform Bangladesh’s social protection system through direct cash transfers, integrated databases and employment-focused welfare policies, while also acknowledging long-standing irregularities in beneficiary selection and weak institutional capacity.
In an interview with Dhaka Tribune, the BNP leader and first-time minister spoke about nepotism in welfare programs, reforms in the Family Card Project, accessibility for persons with disabilities and the challenges she faced after taking office.
Farzana Sharmin Putul: It is a combination of many things. I cannot deny the influence of my father, but the party’s trust and my own work also played important roles. If my father had not guided me, if the party had not supported me, or if I had not worked sincerely among the people, I would not be here today.
My father has had the biggest influence on me. I closely observed his political journey and principles. I believe if I can follow the path he showed, there is no need to create something entirely different. I am trying to continue that politics of positive change in today’s context.
One of the biggest problems in the past was nepotism in preparing beneficiary lists. Another major issue was that the card might be in one person’s name, but the mobile banking account belonged to someone else. As a result, the money went elsewhere. We are now identifying these problems and trying to remove middlemen through direct transfers using the G2P system and integrated social protection platforms.
Whenever we receive complaints, we investigate immediately. A lot of information is still collected manually, so mistakes happen at the field level. Sometimes a person with a concrete house is listed as living in a temporary house. We are working to correct such errors, but I also believe honesty at the field-administration level is crucial.
We do not yet have a centralized data center where all information can be accessed instantly, but we are moving in that direction. We are trying to create a “family tree” database by coordinating information from different ministries so benefits can be distributed more effectively and duplication can be avoided.
Over the next five years, we want to collect information on around four crore people. The goal is not only to provide allowances, but also to help people become self-sufficient through employment and skill development.
Social protection programs can have political impact, but voters are much more aware now. Our objective is human development, not vote-bank politics. If several families in a village improve their lives, the entire village benefits.
In many cases, there is effectively nothing. Even ministry buildings lack ramps and proper washrooms. We are working to improve accessibility in buildings and transportation systems while also focusing on legal support, skill development and employment opportunities for persons with disabilities.
Yes, that culture must change. Once information is directly linked to the database and NID system, benefits can go straight to the recipient without political recommendations or interference.
Absolutely. We do not want people dependent on allowances. Financial assistance should give them confidence and help them stand on their own feet. We are introducing training programs and promoting initiatives like “one village, one product” to create local employment opportunities.
Our approach has three stages: first food and basic education, then skill development, and finally employment. We are reviewing ongoing projects and focusing on quality rather than quantity.
The condition of many correction centers is extremely poor. In some cases, those responsible for correction also need correction. We are currently reviewing the institutions and identifying where reforms are needed.
What seemed problematic from outside appeared even worse once inside. There are complications at many levels of administration. A culture built over 17 years cannot be changed in just three months. But we are trying to bring the state closer to the people and gradually change that mindset.

item.title: PM visits slain child's Pallabi home
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Thursday night visited the home of the seven-year-old girl brutally killed in a rape and murder incident in capital’s Pallabi.
He arrived at the family’s residence in Block B of Section 11 in Mirpur at around 9:45pm, shortly after a cabinet meeting. During the visit, he met the grieving parents, spoke with them, and offered his condolences to the bereaved family.
According to police, the victim child's body was recovered on Tuesday morning from beneath a bed inside a neighbour’s flat. Her severed head was later found in a bathroom. A murder case was subsequently filed at Pallabi Police Station.
Law enforcement officials first detained the wife of the prime accused, identified as Swapna Akter. Later, the main suspect, Sohel Rana, was arrested in connection with the case. He was subsequently produced before a court, where he reportedly gave a confessional statement admitting to the rape and killing of the child.
The incident has sparked widespread public outrage across Bangladesh, with human chains, protest rallies and demonstrations held in Dhaka and several districts, demanding swift justice and the maximum punishment for those involved.

item.title: Metro rail to run during holidays, except Eid day
item.description:
Dhaka Mass Transit Company Limited (DMTCL) has announced a special metro rail schedule for the upcoming Eid-ul-Azha holidays, with services to remain suspended only on Eid day.
According to a schedule published on Thursday, metro rail services in the capital will operate under limited timings and fixed headways to ensure passenger convenience during the holiday period.
The government has declared a seven-day holiday for Eid-ul-Azha from May 25 to May 31, while Eid is expected to be celebrated on May 28 (Thursday).
Under the special schedule, the first train from Uttara North Station will depart at 6:30am, while the first train from Motijheel Station will leave at 7:15am. The last train from Uttara North will depart at 9:30pm, and the final train from Motijheel Station will leave at 10:10pm.
Authorities said trains will operate throughout the day within the fixed schedule, maintaining headways of 12 to 15 minutes, according to a DMTCL press release.
Around 140 trips are planned using seven train sets, with services to be adjusted depending on passenger demand.
Under the arrangement, passengers will be able to purchase single-journey tickets and recharge MRT and Rapid Pass cards from 6:40am to 9:20am. Rapid Pass cards will also be available at all stations during these hours.
On Fridays, ticket sales at Uttara North Station will begin at 2:45pm, while sales at Motijheel Station will start at 3:05pm.
Authorities further said all ticket counters and vending machines will be closed after 9:20pm.

item.title: Rafi murder: Main accused among three arrested
item.description:
Police have arrested three accused, including the prime suspect Md Imon alias “Baburchi Imon”, in connection with the murder of Md Rafi in Lalbagh’s Shahidnagar area of the capital.
Authorities have also recovered nine rounds of ammunition from a house in Keraniganj linked to the killing.
Police said on Thursday that Rafi was shot at close range by unidentified assailants near the entrance of Lane 3 in Shahidnagar on the night of May 14. Locals later rushed him to Dhaka Medical College Hospital with the help of his family.
He succumbed to his injuries while undergoing treatment on the morning of May 20.
Following the incident, police launched an immediate operation to arrest those involved. Acting on intelligence, officers arrested two suspects, Kana Shahabuddin and Rezaul, from different areas of the capital on May 18.
Based on information obtained from the detainees and further confidential leads, police later tracked down the prime suspect Imon. He was arrested in a raid in Cox’s Bazar Sadar on May 20.
During interrogation, Imon led investigators to a house in Keraniganj, where police recovered nine rounds of pistol ammunition allegedly used in the murder.
DMP’s Deputy Commissioner of Media and Public Relations, NM Nasiruddin, confirmed that a total of three people directly involved in the killing have so far been arrested.
He added that the investigation is ongoing to uncover the full details behind the incident.

item.title: Defending national anthem: Youth entrepreneur Al Hasan Milad released on bail
item.description:
Bangladeshi young entrepreneur Al Hasan Milad was released on April 30, 2026.
In 2025, he experienced controversy by defending the retention of the current national anthem of Bangladesh.
Since the incident started on August 5, there have been various questions about changing the national anthem of Bangladesh that it is written by any poet of Bangladesh and not written by Rabindranath Tagore.
Bangladeshi Islamic scholar Ahmadullah and a few others, during the interim government tenure led by Dr Muhammad Yunus, heavily criticized and advocated for banning Bangladesh's national anthem “Amar Shonar Bangla.”
He said that the national anthem does not have the name of Bangladesh, that the music does not know about Bangladesh, that the music that was created before the birth of Bangladesh should be banned. This argument was opposed by many, including Al Hasan Milad.
Many continued to present various arguments based on that. Maintaining the national anthem, a person presented an argument and posted it on Facebook with arguments on various topics including religious issues.
Milad supported and supported the national anthem and copied it and posted it. But without spreading the entire post, some took his post out of context and instigated a social media trial against him.
He was later taken to the cantonment for safety, but still had to apologize. Even after apologizing, a lawsuit was filed against him and his academic studies came to a halt.
He spent 11 months and 14 days in prison, claiming to protect his country’s national anthem while protecting the constitution of 1972.
Sources said that Al Hasan Milad, who was arrested, was originally opposed to Jamaat-e-Islam and was an active activist of Awami League. From August 5 onwards, he is alleged to have provided money in various places to continue the activities of Awami League and he also helped to continue the online work.
Speaking to Al Hasan Milad, he said that according to Article 4(2) of the Constitution of Bangladesh, insulting the national anthem or intentionally defaming it is punishable by serious punishment, which amounts to treason.
“But I had to spend more than 11 months in jail for defending the national anthem of the country. My education time was wasted. But the main issue was non-payment of extortion because I was demanded to pay Tk10 lakh, but I did not agree. I complained about it to the police, but no one listened to me, for which I had to stay in jail for so long,” he added.

item.title: Easy loans pushing families into silent debt crisis
item.description:
For generations, borrowing money in Bangladesh was considered a last resort -- a carefully calculated decision tied to building a house, funding education or expanding a business.
Today, debt has become a routine part of everyday consumption.
Driven by mobile banking apps, aggressive credit card marketing, instant “Buy Now, Pay Later” offers and rapidly expanding digital loan platforms, borrowing is increasingly being normalized among middle-class and lower-income families alike.
But economists and financial analysts warn that the easy availability of credit is quietly pushing thousands of households into chronic debt traps with potentially dangerous long-term economic consequences.
The concern is no longer limited to isolated financial hardship. Experts say a growing culture of consumption-based borrowing -- often without basic financial planning -- is eroding household savings, increasing dependency on revolving debt and exposing families to severe financial shocks.
The problem, analysts say, begins with the illusion of affordability.
Retailers and lenders increasingly market expensive smartphones, motorcycles and consumer electronics through small monthly installment plans that appear manageable individually.
But multiple overlapping installment payments rapidly consume disposable household income.
“People focus on the monthly payment, not the total liability,” one financial analyst noted in the report.
Once most of a family’s monthly earnings are diverted toward debt repayment, even minor disruptions -- illness, job loss or inflation -- can trigger cascading financial distress.
The rapid expansion of credit cards and personal loans in urban Bangladesh has further accelerated the problem.
Commercial banks and non-bank financial institutions have simplified approval procedures to capture market share, but many borrowers lack a clear understanding of compound interest, revolving credit systems and hidden penalties.
Many cardholders routinely pay only the “minimum amount due,” believing it protects them from additional costs. In reality, unpaid balances continue accumulating high commercial interest daily, causing debt burdens to balloon within months.
Analysts warn that many consumers are now using new loans simply to repay older debts -- a classic indicator of debt entrapment.
The problem is spreading beyond cities.
In rural Bangladesh, farmers, fishermen and small entrepreneurs are increasingly falling into overlapping microcredit liabilities as environmental shocks, crop failures, flooding and seasonal income disruptions make repayments difficult.
According to the report, many borrowers facing defaults are abandoning homes, selling farming equipment below market prices or turning to informal moneylenders charging even higher interest rates just to avoid institutional recovery actions.
Financial stress is also producing social and psychological consequences.
Experts warn that chronic debt is increasingly linked to anxiety, domestic conflict and workplace instability as families struggle under mounting repayment pressure.
Another growing concern is the rise of unauthorized digital loan applications operating outside the oversight of the Bangladesh Telecommunication Regulatory Commission and Bangladesh Bank.
These apps offer instant documentation-free loans but often demand extensive access to users’ phones, including contact lists, photographs and personal data.
According to cybersecurity experts, some operators later use that information to blackmail or publicly shame borrowers who fail to repay on time.
Analysts warn that unless Bangladesh improves consumer financial literacy and strengthens oversight of digital lending, today’s growing household debt pressures could evolve into broader economic vulnerabilities.
Experts are now calling for structured financial literacy programs in schools and stronger regulation of consumer lending platforms before the expanding culture of easy borrowing turns into a deeper social and financial crisis.

item.title: Man who chose conscience over privilege
item.description:
Imagine inheriting every privilege society could offer -- wealth, caste, influence and unquestioned social authority -- and then spending your entire life dismantling the very system that granted those privileges. That was the contradiction at the heart of Raja Ram Mohan Roy.
Born 254 years ago, Roy did not simply challenge the world around him. He attempted to reconstruct it.
Born on May 22, 1772, in Radhanagar in Bengal’s Hooghly district, Ram Mohan Roy came from a prosperous and deeply orthodox Brahmin family. The path before him was already written: preserve tradition, protect privilege and defend the social order. Instead, he chose confrontation over comfort.
By the age of thirty, he had mastered Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic, Bengali and English. He studied the Quran, the Bible and the Upanishads not to prove one wrong and another right, but to search for a larger truth. At a time when most people lived within the boundaries of village and custom, Roy was constructing an intellectual world that crossed religion, language and empire. He was not simply educated; he was one of the sharpest minds of the 19th century.
But what made him extraordinary was not knowledge alone. It was what he chose to do with it.
No chapter of Roy’s life defines him more than his campaign against Sati -- the practice in which widows were forced, pressured or manipulated into immolating themselves on their husbands’ funeral pyres. In 19th-century Bengal, the practice was defended in the language of devotion and religious duty. Roy stripped away that language and called it what he believed it truly was: violence against women.
He protested publicly, petitioned relentlessly and carried the issue to the highest offices of the East India Company. His advocacy eventually reached Governor-General William Bentinck, leading to the Bengal Sati Regulation XVII of 1829, which formally abolished the practice.
Roy did not stop there.
He also campaigned against child marriage, polygamy and the purdah system while arguing that women deserved equal inheritance rights -- ideas considered dangerously radical in his time.
In 1828, he founded the Brahmo Samaj, a reformist movement promoting monotheism, rational inquiry and social justice within Hindu society.
It rejected caste orthodoxy and ritual excess, arguing that religion should deepen humanity rather than bury it beneath tradition.
The movement later became one of the intellectual foundations of the Bengal Renaissance.
Writers, educators and reformers across Bengal -- including regions that now form Bangladesh -- inherited ideas Roy helped place into public life.
He also understood the power of journalism long before modern political movements fully grasped it.
Through newspapers such as Sambad Kaumudi and Mirat-ul-Akbar, Roy used the press to challenge authority and shape public debate.
When the British imposed press restrictions in 1823, he protested openly, arguing that freedom of speech and freedom of religion were not privileges granted by rulers, but natural rights belonging to all people.
More than two centuries later, debates around gender rights, religious pluralism, freedom of expression and social reform continue to shape public life across South Asia.
That is why Raja Ram Mohan Roy no longer feels like a distant historical figure.
He feels unfinished, a standard the present still struggles to reach.
His legacy lies not only in the laws he changed or the institutions he founded, but in the courage of his vision: the belief that privilege carries responsibility, and that education means little if it is not used to challenge injustice.
